newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Crude Outlook - Sellers face flagging demand.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Sellers face flagging demand.

text.p: Slack buying interest is expected to put pressure on market differentials for Middle East crudes this week, despite the cuts in the latest official selling prices (OSPs), traders said Monday.
Last week, Gulf producers trimmed the OSPs of their main grades, prompting the differential between the most recent OSPs and the Dubai value for the month of April to narrow by eight to 28 cents.
Traders say, however, that the reduction was not sharp enough to stimulate flagging buying interest in Middle East crudes.
Most traders said the few remaining barrels of June-loading Gulf crudes were likely to continue to trade at discount levels similar to last week.
"Sure the OSP/Dubai differential is narrower after the latest cut, but there just isn't any demand in the market right now for (Middle East) crudes," one Japanese trader said.
Late last week traders estimated that there were about two to three million barrels of June Abu Dhabi crude grades still looking for buyers in the market.
Traders assessed key Abu Dhabi grades of Murban and Lower Zakum at about OSP minus 20 cents.
"I don't see any buyers, but if there are any they're going to be able to name any price they pretty much want," a second trader said.
Most Qatari and Omani crude oil for June loading are believed to have been placed.

Market participants said Japanese refineries were unlikely to make any fresh purchases of Middle East crudes given their high stocks of kerosene and gas oil, which coupled with seasonally low demand is sapping buying interest.
Japan's kerosene stocks stood at 2.4 million kilolitres (kl) at the end of March according to the most recent government import data, up 37.4 percent from a year earlier.
Its gas oil stocks stood at 2.2 million kl at the the of March, up 34.9 percent from the comparable period in 1996.
It was not clear if any of the U.S. majors, which often buy Middle East crudes, would make any new purchases.
China, another key market player, traditionally does not buy much Abu Dhabi crude.

Moreover, it has been conspicuously buying large volumes of West African crudes taking advantage of the narrow Brent/Dubai differential which makes the purchase of West African cargoes financially attractive.
The Brent/Dubai differential remains narrow keeping open the potential for arbitrage of West African barrels of crude, traders say.
Traders estimated early last week that China had purchased about 4.5 million barrels of West African crudes loading in the first half of June.
It bought a range of crude grades including Cabinda, Zafiro, Palanca and Mandji.
In the Asian crude market last week buying interest was seen for Bach Ho cargoes.
At least four June Bach Ho cargoes were believed sold by Japanese trading companies at premiums of betwen 19 cents to 30 cents above the official selling price.
